title: Individual generative-AI access changes email and after-hours work patterns before detectable task redesign
source_unit: knowledge worker-week in a randomized field experiment across participating firms
geography: United States; participating firms and workers in the study

observations.period: Six-month experiment; NBER Working Paper 33795, issued 2025 and revised November 2025

denominator.unit: knowledge workers across 66 firms; approximately half selected for AI-tool access

treatment_design.value: workers were randomly selected to receive access to a generative-AI tool integrated into email, meetings, and writing applications

tool_take_up.unit: percent of treated workers who used the tool in the current NBER abstract

email_time.value: about two fewer hours per week among treated users in the current NBER abstract

task_quantity_composition.value: no detected shift from individual-level provision

observations.method: Randomized field experiment with six-month worker-level digital activity outcomes; treatment assignment and tool use are distinct estimands.
observations.uncertainty: The experiment covers participating firms, knowledge workers, one integrated tool, and a six-month window. The current NBER abstract reports about two fewer email hours among treated users; the public revised abstract reports 3.6 fewer hours among frequent users and a 1.3-hour intent-to-treat estimate. These summaries use different denominators and are not pooled.
observations.subgroup: Participating knowledge workers; detailed effects by occupation, industry, demographic group, family responsibility, and managerial status are not promoted in this record.
observations.counterinterpretation: Less email or after-hours time can reflect task assistance, substitution into other work, changed reporting, or temporary novelty; it does not identify lower total workload, greater autonomy, or household benefit.

observations.period: Six-month experiment; public revised abstract version

frequent_user_email_time.unit: fewer hours per week among workers who used the tool in more than half of sample weeks

intent_to_treat_email_time.unit: fewer hours per week; assignment-based estimate

observations.method: Public revised abstract associated with the NBER paper; abstract-level extraction, not a re-estimation.
observations.uncertainty: The user-effect and assignment-effect denominators differ; the abstract does not by itself show whether saved time became rest, care, additional work, or higher expectations.
observations.subgroup: Frequent tool users versus assignment group; no general population inference.
observations.counterinterpretation: Unchanged meeting time may reflect coordination constraints, but it does not prove that meetings are unaffected by later organizational adaptation.

related_sources.claim: Task-level worker-reported adoption is uneven among workers doing similar work; exposure is not adoption.
Repeated US surveys provide population-level generative-AI adoption and assisted-hour context.
A separate experiment tests digital surveillance and managerial explanation, keeping control and AI assistance distinct.

boundary: This record promotes a randomized worker-level time-pattern result from a defined field experiment. It does not establish firm productivity, job redesign, worker authority, pay, health, household time, political meaning, or geopolitical consequence. Access, take-up, task change, coordination, and control remain separate stages.
